Tone languages are further distinguished as register tone languages and contour tone languages. ... On the contrary, in a contour tone language, to which Bongcher belongs, there are successive levels of pitch fluctuation, i.e., the various tones include some in which the essential feature is a changing pitch (Pike, 1948). Bongcher shows a two way tone contrast; some of the vowels are pronounced with the pitch lower than the average while the others are pronounced with the pitch higher than the average. The tone which is lower than the average might be termed as low or falling tone and that which is higher than the average as high or rising tone. new_statements.rule_in_words: Bongcher (a Halam variety) is analysed as a contour tone language with a two-way lexical tone contrast (falling/low vs rising/high, e.g. lùŋ 'heart' vs lúŋ 'stone'), explicitly classed as a tone language rather than a stress language; the description gives no location for word stress. Debbarma 2017 (Korbong grammar, ch.3 sec.3.2 pp.12-13) and Debbarma 2018 (Hrangkhawl, ch.3 sec.3.3) independently report two lexical tones (high/low) and are likewise silent on stress; Kharlukhi 2012 (ch.5 p.37) instead says Ranglong-Halam 'do[es] not have tone' and also says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Chaudhuri notes tones do not occur on /ə/ and that the tonal contrast is clearer in monosyllables than in words of two or more syllables (LII article sec.7 / thesis conclusion); no stress-related exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word level tone on syllables in citation forms; no phrase-level prosody discussed. Variety: Bongcher dialect (Glottolog bong1300) of Halam rang1267, data from Tripura.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Bongcher variety (Glottolog dialect bong1300 under rang1267 Halam), fieldwork in Tripura. Corroborating tone-only descriptions: Korbong/Karbong (Debbarma 2017; a Halam sub-tribe of c.117 speakers, Khowai/West Tripura -- Glottolog files this grammar under rang1267 but lists no separate Korbong dialect code) and Tripura Hrangkhawl (Debbarma 2018; = Glottolog hran1240 'Hrangkhol (Halam)' under rang1267, distinct from language-level hran1239). Kharlukhi 2012's 'Halam' is Ranglong-Halam (rang1271), which she describes as non-tonal. No source opened describes stress for any Halam variety; Ranglong proper (the ISO rnl reference name) has only morphosyntax papers and tone-marked texts open online.
